title: Give each report plugin its own libraries and the server's API

blocks.text: The report server runs exporters that customers write themselves. Each plugin arrives as a jar built with everything it was compiled against: the server's plugin API and the libraries the customer tested with, which are often older or newer than the server's own copies.

Two attempts have shipped so far. The first gave every plugin its own `URLClassLoader` with no link to the server, and the server could no longer use a single plugin: every one failed with `ClassCastException` on the line that hands it to the scheduler. The second made the server's loader the parent, and a customer's ledger export began formatting numbers the way the server's version of their formatting library does, not the way the version in their jar does.

`PluginLoader` already knows what the jar holds (`inBundle`), which classes are the server's API (`isApi`), and how to define a class from the jar (`defineFromBundle`). Finish the `TODO` in `src/main/java/practice/PluginLoader.java`: `loadClass(...)`, which decides what each class name the plugin uses resolves to.

When you're done, the server can use every plugin through the API types it knows, each plugin runs on the library versions in its own jar, and anything the jar doesn't carry, the JDK included, comes from the server. About eight lines in total.
The tests build a plugin jar in memory from compiled classes, so its classes have the same names as classes the server already has.

cases.says: the plugin class loads from its jar and runs, and JDK classes resolve through the loader
the server can cast the plugin to the API interface it knows, although the plugin's jar carries a copy of that interface
the plugin runs on the version of a library its jar carries, not on the server's version of the same class
asking the loader for a class it has already loaded returns that class again rather than failing

origin.section: A Class Is Its Name Plus the Loader That Defined It

concepts: A loader defines a name once: defining it again is a LinkageError, and a custom loader can't define a java.* class.

A class is identified by its name and its defining loader, so a plugin loader that defines its own copy of the host's interface produces objects the host can't cast to it, while parent-first delegation gives both sides one class.
